title: Glasshouse and Postcards
premise: Theo Okafor, a bridge inspector whose marriage has quietly corroded like the steel she measures, hears an unrecorded song on the radio — one her late mother wrote and never released — sung by a stranger who claims it as his own. Chasing him, Theo uncovers that her mother survived a fire that killed another woman, taking her identity, her songs, and her silence with her. As Theo's marriage reaches its own demolition date, she must decide whether love built on concealment can bear load, forgiving both the stranger in the old photographs and the mother who became her. In the end, Theo records the song under her mother's true name, files for divorce not in anger but in honesty, and walks the new span of the rebuilt bridge carrying nothing she cannot say aloud.
about_author: Silas Ishikawa is a former structural engineer who spent nine years inspecting bridges along the Ohio River before turning to fiction full-time. His work examines the quiet mechanics of things that hold — marriages, families, steel — and the precise moment they fail.

chapters.title: Expansion Joints
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. On the Harlow Street Bridge, Theo measures gaps in steel the way she no longer measures words at home; her husband Marcus talks past her over dinner about a promotion she never agreed to want. The beat: competent numbness, a marriage inspected but unrepaired.

chapters.title: The Song That Wasn't
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. Driving home through rain, a radio station plays a song her mother hummed only to herself — a song Theo knows was never recorded. She pulls over, shaking, and calls the station. The DJ says the artist's name: Daniel Voss. The beat: vertigo, the past breaching the present.

chapters.title: Daniel Voss
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. She finds Voss playing a small club and confronts him afterward; he claims their mother taught him the song in 1991, showing a photograph of a woman Theo doesn't recognize wearing her mother's coat. The beat: confrontation curdling into doubt — which woman is the stranger?

chapters.title: What the Photographs Keep
chapters.summary: Alternating POV, Theo and flashbacks from her mother Adaeze's letters. Theo searches the attic and finds photographs of two young women, one clearly her mother, one unlabeled, plus a postcard dated three days before a boarding-house fire in Wheeling that killed one occupant. The beat: dread dressed as curiosity.

chapters.title: Marcus Notices
chapters.summary: Marcus's POV. Watching Theo disappear into boxes and phone calls, Marcus feels the familiar relief of her distraction — he's been hiding something too, a job offer in another city accepted without discussion. The beat: guilt mirrored, both spouses keeping ledgers.

chapters.title: Wheeling, 1989
chapters.summary: Adaeze's POV (letters/diary). Flashback chapter: young Adaeze arrives at the boarding house, befriends Ruth Calloway, a local songwriter, and begins performing Ruth's songs under encouragement that shades into dependence. The beat: warmth before theft, friendship as foreshadowing.

chapters.title: The Fire Report
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. Theo obtains the fire investigation file: one death, Ruth Calloway; Adaeze listed among survivors, then gone from all records within a month. A coroner's note questions the identification. The beat: cold procedural horror, the state's paper trail contradicting family myth.

chapters.title: Load Rating
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. Back on the bridge, Theo finds hairline cracking in a girder her last report passed; her supervisor pressures her to sign off anyway because demolition is scheduled and litigation looms. She refuses. The beat: her professional integrity sharpening into a personal ethic she must apply to her own history.

chapters.title: Ruth's Sister
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. Theo tracks down Ruth's sister, Eleanor, now elderly, who has spent thirty years believing Adaeze died in the fire — the body was identified by Adaeze's coat, worn by Ruth. Eleanor's grief turns to fury at the sight of Theo. The beat: inherited guilt made flesh; Theo becomes her mother's face.

chapters.title: Almost Saying It
chapters.summary: Marcus's POV. Marcus tries to confess about the job offer over an anniversary dinner Theo misses to meet Eleanor; he almost says it, practices the art of almost saying it, and instead gives her a gift chosen for the woman he married twelve years ago. The beat: tenderness weaponized by avoidance.

chapters.title: The Coat
chapters.summary: Eleanor's POV. Eleanor recounts the night of the fire: Ruth went back inside for her songbook; Adaeze stood outside in Ruth's coat, in shock, and let the responders assume. Whether she intended the swap, even Eleanor cannot say. The beat: ambiguity as the true horror — survival may have been accident, then habit.

chapters.title: Demolition Date
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. The bridge demolition is set; so, Theo realizes, is her marriage — Marcus's transfer date, the house listing he secretly arranged, everything converging on the same week. She confronts him; the fight they've deferred for years finally happens. The beat: rupture as release.

chapters.title: Voss's Version
chapters.summary: Daniel's POV. Daniel reveals his side: Adaeze, dying, gave him the songs and made him promise to get them heard, knowing a dead woman's name would open no doors. He recorded 'Glasshouse' under his own name out of cowardice and has regretted it ever since. The beat: complicity examined, another survivor of Adaeze's silences.

chapters.title: The Postcards
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. Theo deciphers the stack of unsent postcards Adaeze wrote to Ruth every year on the fire's anniversary — apologies drafted and never mailed, each one more honest than anything she said aloud to her daughter. The beat: grief for a mother met only in draft form.

chapters.title: Eleanor's Terms
chapters.summary: Eleanor's POV. Eleanor agrees to help Theo restore Ruth's name publicly, but on one condition: Theo must first say plainly what her mother did, without the softening word 'survived.' Theo does, and something loosens between them. The beat: forgiveness beginning as accuracy.

chapters.title: Cracking
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. Under public pressure after Theo's refusal to sign the inspection, the county accelerates the bridge closure; Theo walks the empty span alone at dawn, measuring the cracks she once called hairline, seeing her marriage and her inheritance in them. The beat: solitary reckoning, the inspector inspected.

chapters.title: What Adaeze Carried
chapters.summary: Adaeze's POV (final letter). A last diary entry reveals Adaeze knew Ruth went back for the songbook, knew the coat caused the misidentification, and chose silence because truth meant deportation and ruin — the price of survival paid daily for thirty years. The beat: condemnation and compassion held together.

chapters.title: The Recording
chapters.summary: Theo and Daniel's POV alternating. In a studio, Theo sings 'Glasshouse' — her mother's voice living in hers — and they record it credited to Adaeze Okafor, with Ruth Calloway named as co-writer where the songs began. The beat: restoration, names returned to their owners.

chapters.title: Public Record
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. Theo and Eleanor hold a small ceremony at the Wheeling site; the historical marker is corrected, Ruth's name read aloud, the postcards finally delivered to her grave. Daniel performs. The beat: communal absolution, small and insufficient and real.

chapters.title: The Demolition
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs braided. The Harlow Street Bridge comes down in forty seconds of controlled collapse; Theo watches with Marcus, and they speak honestly for the first time in years — not reconciling, but parting without rubble. The beat: catharsis through destruction done right, on purpose.

chapters.title: New Span
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. Eighteen months later: the replacement bridge opens, Theo signs the final inspection under her own full name, and 'Glasshouse' plays quietly from a passing car radio, credited correctly. Eleanor visits; forgiveness has become ordinary, which is its highest form. The beat: quiet resolution, structures that hold because they're honest.

chapters.title: Postcard, Sent
chapters.summary: Theo's POV, coda. Theo writes a postcard to her mother — finally sent, addressed to a name that was true — saying the thing Adaeze spent a lifetime almost saying: I know what you did, and I know what it cost, and I forgive the stranger in the photographs because she raised me. The beat: completion, the art of almost saying it abandoned at last.
